    {
      "startEvent": 768,

  ],
  "candidates": [
    {
      "startEvent": 683,
      "endEvent": 694,
      "contextStartEvent": 651,
      "contextEndEvent": 712,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "But science has nothing to say about singularities.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "none"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The blanket boundary claim excludes scientific criticism of exceptional events without explaining why regularities cannot constrain their assessment. E686–E694 additionally treats Krauss's rejection as dictated by atheism. Lennox offers an intervention rationale at E674–E682, but that does not establish this exclusion; Krauss explicitly requests testable evidence at E695–E712."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 723,
      "endEvent": 724,
      "contextStartEvent": 695,
      "contextEndEvent": 724,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "and therefore you'd be crazy to be not be an atheist outside of it.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "ridicule"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The closing affirmation converts laboratory practice into a general requirement of atheism. E714–E721 explains why experimenters assume no hand is manipulating their apparatus, but supplies no bridge from that working assumption to atheism outside the laboratory. Earlier requests for miracle evidence provide context, without earning this broader conclusion or expressly immunizing it."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1678,
      "endEvent": 1680,
      "contextStartEvent": 1677,
      "contextEndEvent": 1722,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "god doesn't explain a darn thing. Never has, never will.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "none"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The permanent dismissal may replace an assessment of particular divine explanations, but E1680–E1692 supplies a reason: allegedly unstable or absent definitions. That makes this more than an isolated slogan. Whether 'never will' excludes even adequately specified proposals remains unclear; Lennox supplies his personal-creator specification at E1698–E1722."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1775,
      "endEvent": 1780,
      "contextStartEvent": 1751,
      "contextEndEvent": 1794,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "the fact that it threatens people like you suggests that you have something to be threatened by.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "shame"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Krauss reframes Lennox's objection as evidence of feeling threatened, giving criticism a discrediting psychological interpretation without establishing that reaction. Lennox immediately denies it at E1781. This is a local protective argument, not a settled general catchphrase; E1782–E1794 also returns to the substantive distinction between proving atheism and finding no need for God."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1853,
      "endEvent": 1857,
      "contextStartEvent": 1818,
      "contextEndEvent": 1870,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "don't say it's evidence based. It's based on your reading of a document.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "ridicule"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The wording appears to exclude documentary evidence categorically, which could shield the denial of resurrection evidence from historical testimony. However, the Gatsby comparison at E1862–E1864 may instead challenge whether a document's existence establishes its truth. No historical evidence is examined, so categorical protective use remains uncertain rather than confirmed."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 975,
      "endEvent": 994,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "Of course, your surprise would be that they all missed.",
      "explanation": "The firing-squad analogy explains why surviving to observe an outcome need not explain that outcome. Its application to cosmology is disputable, but the compact conclusion summarizes an explicit argument rather than replacing one."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1327,
      "endEvent": 1345,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "Does that prove that happened? Absolutely not.",
      "explanation": "Krauss separates a model's agreement with observed characteristics from proof of cosmic origins, then acknowledges unknown ultimate laws and speculation. The qualification limits the inference he actually offers."
    }
  ]
